profile.campus: Prineville, Crook County, Oregon (Meta's original data center campus, seven buildings)
profile.address: Southwest Houston Lake Road, Prineville, Crook County, Oregon, 97554
profile.reading:
This is the northern and larger of the two Meta buildings that this registry maps on the western edge of the company's Prineville data center campus in Crook County, Oregon. It sits on the high desert bench west of the city, on ground the county carries as light industrial. Crook County taxlot records place both of these buildings on map taxlot 1515000000301, account 19980, a 244.53 acre parcel zoned M1 and owned by Vitesse LLC, a Meta holding entity whose mailing address in the county roll is 1 Hacker Way, Menlo Park, California. Vitesse LLC holds nine taxlots in Crook County totalling roughly 488 acres, including one with a situs address of 3201 SW Houston Lake Road and others fronting Meta named streets such as SW Connect Way and SW Social Loop, which is a fair measure of how much ground the campus has taken in since the first building broke ground in 2010.

Meta publishes campus figures for Prineville rather than building figures. The company reports more than 2 billion dollars invested since 2010, more than 350 operational jobs once the campus is complete, about 1,000 skilled trade workers on site at peak construction, more than 5.7 million dollars in direct funding to Crook County schools and nonprofits and more than 400 local grants and sponsorships since 2011, LEED Gold certification for operational buildings, electricity use matched with clean and renewable energy including support for three Oregon projects adding 220 megawatts of new generation, and commitments to restore 200 percent of the water the campus consumes and to be water positive in 2030. When Meta announced in March 2021 that Prineville was growing again, it described two more buildings, about 900,000 square feet of added space, and a finished campus of eleven buildings and nearly 4.6 million square feet. It does not publish square footage, power draw or commissioning dates for individual buildings, so this page cannot say which construction phase this particular structure belongs to. What the map does show is that it is roughly twice the footprint of its southern neighbor on the same taxlot.

Prineville also carries the campus's one genuinely historic claim. In April 2011 Facebook published the design of the first Prineville building and of the servers inside it, reporting a power usage effectiveness of 1.07 against roughly 1.5 for conventional practice at the time, 38 percent less energy than the company's existing leased facilities and 24 percent lower infrastructure cost, and released the mechanical and electrical drawings as the founding contribution to the Open Compute Project. Prineville is where that argument was first made in concrete and steel.

What is not known matters as much. No operator statement or Oregon filing reviewed for this page states an IT load for this building or for the campus, and none states a contracted utility service level. Any single megawatt number attached to Prineville in a commercial directory should be treated as unsourced until an operator or a utility filing says otherwise.

profile.capacity_note: Prineville publishes nothing that fixes any of the four power quantities for this building. it_capacity_mw is absent because no operator statement or filing gives an IT load. utility_power_mw is absent because no Pacific Power or Oregon PUC filing reviewed here states a contracted service level for the campus or for this building. No standby diesel rating and no on site generation are established either. Megawatt figures that appear against Prineville in commercial directories are directory estimates rather than operator or utility numbers, and a service size, if one were published, would still not be an IT load.
profile.facility_note: Meta Prineville, Oregon: the birthplace of the Open Compute Project (2011), Meta's original hyperscale data center campus, seven buildings, $2B+ invested since a 2010 groundbreaking.
profile.research_note: Facility page rebuilt 2026-09-05 from operator, county and state primary records. Ownership traced to Vitesse LLC through the Crook County taxlot layer, incentive terms taken from a Business Oregon project table filed with the Oregon Legislature, and the utility and tax policy record taken from Oregon PUC and legislative sources.
profile.community_note: Water has been the central local question. Prineville built an aquifer storage recovery system that injects surplus winter groundwater for recovery during summer peaks. Apple funded the first well with an 8.7 million dollar grant in 2019 and Meta has funded a second, together intended to bank about 300 million gallons a year. City figures reported in 2024 put Meta's Prineville water use at 117.5 million gallons in 2020 falling to 68.4 million gallons in 2022, with later reporting citing about 70 million gallons in 2024, and city officials describing data centers as using around 10 percent of Prineville's water on the roughly ten hottest days of the year. Meta reports more than 5.7 million dollars in direct funding to Crook County schools and nonprofits and more than 400 local grants and sponsorships since 2011. Local reporting counts roughly 700 people employed across Prineville's data centers.
profile.incentives_note: Meta's Crook County holdings are in the Prineville and Crook County Long Term Rural Enterprise Zone, which carries a 15 year property tax exemption. A Business Oregon project table prepared for the Oregon Legislature in October 2019 lists Facebook data centers under Vitesse LLC in Crook County with two operating facilities, 27,780,605 dollars in taxes foregone in 2017-18, 300,000 dollars in locally agreed fees in 2018 and 177 jobs, alongside a further approved facility with anticipated investment above 200 million dollars. Apple's two Crook County facilities appear on the same table with a 15 year term, 17,605,121 dollars foregone and 350,000 dollars in fees. Later local reporting puts total exempted value in Crook County above 130 million dollars in 2025-26 and cites a Good Jobs First analysis finding roughly 29 million dollars in county school revenue foregone in 2024 against about 10 million dollars in 2019. Prineville's city manager has said the city expects to roughly double its property tax revenue when Meta's first enterprise zone agreement expires in 2027.
profile.regulatory_note: Two Oregon changes now bear on data centers in Crook County. Under the POWER Act, House Bill 3546 of 2025, the Public Utility Commission has required utilities to create a separate rate class for very large loads. The commission approved Portland General Electric's Schedule 96 in docket UM 2377, which includes a one cent per kilowatt hour surcharge for customers above 100 megawatts of allocated system capacity, with the proceeds directed to residential bill relief. PacifiCorp, which serves Prineville, filed its own proposal on March 30, 2026 in Advice 26-009 for a Schedule 401 covering new large energy use facilities, applying above 20 megawatts with separate treatment above 100 megawatts and carrying minimum utilization, contract term and early termination provisions. Separately, House Bill 4084, effective June 5, 2026, bars new data centers from Oregon's enterprise zone property tax exemption until 90 days after the 2027 legislative session adjourns. Facilities already receiving the exemption, and those already approved while in planning or construction, keep it, and the Strategic Investment Program is unaffected.
profile.campus_power_note: Prineville sits in Pacific Power (PacifiCorp) territory. Meta reports that its Prineville electricity use is matched with clean and renewable energy and that it is supporting three Oregon projects adding 220 megawatts of new generation, which is a procurement and matching arrangement rather than a statement of the campus service size. No campus level megawatt figure for delivered power has been published by Meta or by the utility.

reading.body:
Prineville is Meta's original hyperscale data center campus, seven buildings mapped here on 488 acres of M1-zoned ground west of the city in Crook County, part of an eleven-building, 4.6 million square foot campus announced complete in 2021 after a groundbreaking in 2010. Meta has invested more than two billion dollars and published no IT load, utility service level, or per-building power figure for any structure on the site, so the campus capacity cannot be stated in megawatts. The company reports electricity use matched with clean and renewable energy including support for three Oregon projects adding 220 megawatts of new generation, a procurement arrangement that does not define the campus service size. No operator statement or Oregon utility filing reviewed here establishes how much power Prineville draws or how much of the high desert's available grid capacity it occupies.

This building, the northern and larger of two structures on a single 244-acre taxlot, sits in Pacific Power territory under a 15-year property tax exemption now set to expire in 2027. PacifiCorp filed a new rate schedule in March 2026 that will apply to large new facilities above 20 megawatts, with separate treatment and minimum contract terms for loads above 100 megawatts, establishing the utility's expectation that future builds in this corridor will be disclosed. Prineville's own water use fell from 117.5 million gallons in 2020 to 68.4 million gallons in 2022, and the city has constructed an aquifer storage and recovery system funded by both Meta and Apple to bank roughly 300 million gallons annually. The enterprise zone agreement that sheltered Prineville's first decades of expansion will lapse before the campus's full buildout is complete, signaling a shift in the incentive environment for large loads in Oregon.

In April 2011, Meta published the design of Prineville's first building and its servers, claiming 1.07 power usage effectiveness against 1.5 for conventional practice, releasing the mechanical and electrical drawings, and naming the undertaking the Open Compute Project. That foundational moment in hyperscale design doctrine occurred in concrete and steel in Crook County. Prineville remains the only campus in Oregon whose published megawatt claim sits above the state median, ranking ninth by stated capacity against 133 mapped facilities statewide. The campus publishes no annual reports, no quarterly filings, and no building-level data that would allow readers to track how much compute density or power draw has materialized inside those steel walls since 2010.
